summary: Collects in one place the syntax (ABNF) changes that many IMAP extensions made to base IMAP commands from RFC 3501. It also suggests patterns for adding options to existing commands so future extensions stay compatible. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4466 brings IMAP extension grammar together in one place and gives future extensions a consistent way to add options to existing commands. It changes how commands are written, not what those commands mean.

questions: how do imap extensions add options to commands
subtitle: One collected grammar for IMAP extensions, with a reusable pattern for adding parameters to existing commands.

tldr.problem: Many IMAP extensions changed the syntax of base commands, leaving their grammar spread across separate documents and in different forms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4466 collects most of those ABNF changes and defines a common tagged-extension pattern for options on existing commands. It also adds an extended SEARCH response called ESEARCH.
tldr.outcome: The RFC changes syntax, not command semantics, and updates the ABNF in RFCs 2088, 2342, 3501, 3502 and 3516. It has since been updated by RFC 6237 and RFC 7377.

facts.label: Commands extended
facts.value: SELECT, EXAMINE, CREATE, RENAME, FETCH, STORE, SEARCH and APPEND

today: RFC 4466 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 6237 and RFC 7377. The RFC says its ABNF was expected to be incorporated into a future revision of RFC 3501.

sections.title: Why Collect IMAP Grammar
sections.content:
Over time, IMAP extensions added syntax to the base commands in RFC 3501. RFC 4466 collects most of those Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) changes so readers and implementers do not have to find each extension's grammar separately.

The document also generalizes the grammar and defines building blocks for compatible future extensions. It updates ABNF in RFCs 2088, 2342, 3501, 3502 and 3516, but does not specify semantic changes to those documents.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP command rules had been spread across many extension documents. This RFC gathers the grammar and makes the extension patterns more consistent without changing what commands do.

sections.title: The Tagged-Extension Pattern
sections.content:
The recommended pattern for future extensions is tagged-ext: a tagged label followed by a value. Labels begin with a letter, hyphen, underscore or period, and may continue with those characters, digits or a colon.

The value can be a number or sequence set, or a parenthesized group of components. Components may be nested. This common structure lets a parser identify an extension parameter and handle its value even when it does not implement that extension's meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: An extension parameter starts with a recognizable name, followed by its value. A shared format helps servers parse new options consistently.

sections.title: Adding Parameters to IMAP Commands
sections.content:
The collected grammar adds optional parameters to SELECT, EXAMINE, CREATE and RENAME, and modifiers to FETCH and STORE. The parameter names appear in a parenthesized list at a specified position in each command; their order is arbitrary and their values are optional.

The RFC defines no new parameters for these commands itself. A server must reject a parameter or modifier that it does not support with a BAD response. SELECT and EXAMINE parameters may describe either a session-wide change or a change that lasts only while a mailbox is selected.
sections.plainLanguage: Several IMAP commands gain a place for optional extension settings. A server that does not recognize an option rejects the command rather than guessing what the option means.

sections.title: Extended SEARCH and ESEARCH
sections.content:
Extended SEARCH commands can include a RETURN list of result options before the search criteria. This RFC defines no result options, but it defines a new untagged ESEARCH response for returning search results.

ESEARCH may include a command tag to correlate the response, a UID indicator and one or more name/value result pairs. The UID indicator says whether the returned values refer to UIDs or message numbers. Result pairs may appear in any order, and a return-item name should appear only once unless an extension says otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: ESEARCH labels each kind of search result instead of returning only an unlabelled list. The optional command tag helps the client match the result to its search request.

sections.title: APPEND and Existing Extensions
sections.content:
APPEND has a different extension pattern so it remains compatible with the BINARY and MULTIAPPEND extensions. The common syntax accounts for binary message data and for appending multiple messages atomically when MULTIAPPEND is supported.

The literal8 syntax allows a non-synchronizing literal when the server supports both BINARY and LITERAL+. The RFC also rewrites the ABNF for the NAMESPACE response for readability and updates the STATUS attribute-list production; it states that these changes do not change what is sent on the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: APPEND uses a tailored grammar so earlier extensions for binary data and multiple messages continue to fit. The revised NAMESPACE grammar is reorganized without changing the messages sent.

sections.title: Parser Complexity and Security
sections.content:
Implementations still need to consult the updated extension documents for their security considerations. The RFC notes that complicated grammars can increase parser bugs, including buffer overflows and denial-of-service problems; consistent syntax may make parsers simpler.

Commands allowed before authentication deserve particular care because more potential attackers can reach them and some servers run with elevated privileges in that state. This document does not extend commands in the NOT AUTHENTICATED state.
sections.plainLanguage: More complicated command rules can create more chances for parser mistakes. Consistent syntax helps, and extensions to commands available before login need especially careful design.
